name: PT Kalbe Farma Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Kalbe Farma: a derated healthcare franchise with a margin problem, not a demand problem
frontmatter.summary: Kalbe trades at a multiple usually reserved for declining businesses while every segment is growing. The de-rating is about imported-input margins and rupiah weakness, not about demand for its brands or its distribution reach. We think margin troughs in FY2026E, the buyback is running, and the market is paying well below our bear-case value. Initiate BUY.
thesis: Kalbe is the scale incumbent in Indonesian pharma and consumer health, with a distribution arm that reaches channels smaller manufacturers cannot; the moat is density of reach, not a patent.

The share price de-rated as gross margin fell on imported raw materials and a weak rupiah; management says the pressure lasts to end-2026, which is precisely why the trough is buyable rather than a reason to wait.
Revenue growth is intact across all four segments, and the distribution division is winning external principals, which raises fixed-cost absorption even while the margin line is compressed.
The balance sheet carries net cash, a buyback is in the market, and the stated dividend policy sits far above the payout actually paid in FY2025 — a re-rating lever we do not capitalise.
The main risk is not demand but the rupiah and JKN generic pricing; both are in the bear case, and the price already sits below that bear-case value.

catalysts.event: End of the on-market buyback window
BPOM-hosted Global Health Product Regulatory Science Forum, Bali
FY2026 audited results and FY2027 guidance
Annual general meeting: FY2026 dividend decision against the stated payout policy

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Kalbe Farma Tbk with a BUY and a twelve-month target of Rp1,059, against a last price of Rp755, a total return of 43.0%. The rating is not a call on the rupiah or on JKN pricing; it is a call that the market has applied a distressed multiple to a franchise whose volumes, brands and distribution reach are intact. At 9.3x forward earnings the price discounts a permanent impairment of the margin structure. We think the impairment is cyclical and already visible in the numbers: gross margin fell on imported raw materials and rupiah weakness, management guides that the pressure runs to the end of FY2026, and the segment data show demand growing in every division [S3][S12].

The variant view has three parts. First, the margin story is an input-cost story, not a pricing-power story: management states plainly that rupiah weakness hits gross profit because production costs are heavily import-linked, and that inventory means no significant recovery is visible before the year end [S12]. That is a timing problem with a known cure — selective price increases and a mix shift toward specialty and biologic products are already running [S12]. Second, growth is broad: consolidated sales rose 11.5% in the first nine months of 2026, with prescription up 6.5%, consumer health up 9.9% and distribution and logistics up 21.6% [S3]. Third, the capital return is understated in the base case: the FY2025 dividend resolution paid 25.6% of net profit, far below the company's own stated payout policy, which produced the FY2024 distribution [S14][S11]. We model the resolved payout, not the policy — but we do not count a return to policy as upside: the DCF is FCFF, which contains no payout term, so a higher dividend moves cash from the balance sheet to holders without changing the enterprise value. It improves the cash return and the dividend yield; it is not in the target.

What the market appears to price is a franchise that cannot earn its cost of capital. Our DCF says otherwise: the discounted cash flows are worth Rp1,097 a share at a cost of capital of 12.0%, and the enterprise value that implies is not demanding on terminal profitability [S0]. The two market cross-checks land lower — P/E at Rp644 on the peer median of 7.7x and EV/EBITDA at Rp832 — because the Indonesian pharma peer set contains distressed generic manufacturers whose multiples reflect their own balance sheets, not Kalbe's [S0]. We weight by comparability rather than by distance from the DCF: the DCF takes 55% because the forecast is explicit and the balance sheet is net cash; EV/EBITDA takes 30% because it is capital-structure neutral and Kalbe trades below its peer median on it; and the peer P/E takes only 15%, because a multiple the report itself calls distressed cannot carry a third of the answer. The divergence is explained in the valuation section rather than averaged away.

The two or three things that move the value are therefore simple to monitor. The gross margin line in the quarterly report is the first: the sensitivity grid shows that a hundred basis points of gross margin moves the twelve-month value by a few rupiah a share, material but smaller than the 500 IDR bn buyback's effect on the share count — the margin matters because it is persistent, not because one point of it outweighs the capital return. The rupiah is the second, because it is the input to that margin. The third is the payout decision at the FY2026 annual meeting, where a return to the stated policy would lift the dividend line without changing a single operating assumption. Against that, the price sits below our bear-case value of Rp775, which is the definition of an asymmetric setup rather than a heroic one [S0].

Kalbe is the scale incumbent in Indonesian pharmaceuticals, and the business is best understood as four linked divisions rather than one. In the first half of 2026 the prescription pharmaceuticals division recorded net sales of 5,300 IDR bn, consumer health 2,700 IDR bn, nutritionals 4,260 IDR bn and distribution and logistics 7,200 IDR bn [S12]. The distribution division is the largest single line and the fastest growing, because it does not only move Kalbe's own products: it carries third-party principals, and that external business is what drove its growth in the first nine months of 2026 [S3]. This matters for the investment case because it turns a cost centre into a revenue line and absorbs fixed costs across a wider base.

The prescription business is the franchise's core identity. It supplies branded ethical products and unbranded generics for the national health insurance programme, and management is deliberately widening the specialty portfolio into oncology, biosimilars, insulin and vaccines, supported by newer production facilities including a radiopharmaceutical plant for early cancer detection [S6]. The consumer health division is the brand engine — over-the-counter medicines and supplements — and grew ahead of the group in the first nine months of 2026 on the OTC and supplement categories [S3]. Nutritionals is the most mature and slowest of the four, growing in the low single digits as management shifts the portfolio toward lifestyle and ready-to-drink formats [S3].

The strategy management describes is a barbell. At one end, generics and JKN supply protect volume and national relevance; at the other, specialty and biologic products, cell therapy and vaccines are where the margin is meant to come from over time [S3][S6]. In consumer health and nutrition the lever is brand rejuvenation and preventive-positioned products, which management argues keeps the portfolio relevant to younger consumers [S3]. The company is also localising medical-device assembly to raise domestic content, a policy-linked strategy that is easier in devices than in prescription drugs because local active-ingredient supply remains limited [S12].

The footprint is national manufacturing and distribution with an international business that is small relative to the domestic book. The distribution arm, Enseval Putera Megatrading, is separately listed, which is why a minority interest sits against group profit [S0]. Management has said it is open to delisting that subsidiary if it cannot meet the free-float requirement [S12] — a structural option that would simplify the group but consume cash, and one we treat as a watch item rather than a base-case event.

Ownership is concentrated and family-anchored. The pack's insider series shows 65.0% and institutions 11.7%, while the IDX-registry free float is 38.0% [S0]; the insider and registry definitions overlap and do not sum to a hundred, so we treat the insider figure as the control fact and the registry float as the index definition, and we do not add them. Control sits with the founding family, and day-to-day management is professionalised, with a president director and divisional directors reporting through a corporate secretary function [S4][S11]. That structure has been stable for decades and is not, in itself, a governance concern; the governance questions we do have are about transaction procedure rather than control, and we deal with them in the governance section.

Kalbe is a leader, not a challenger, and the competitive position rests on three things that are hard to replicate: the breadth of its brand portfolio across price points, the reach of its own distribution network into general trade and pharmacy channels, and the scale of its manufacturing base, which lets it serve JKN volumes at a cost smaller producers cannot match. None of those is a patent moat, and none of them prevents a competitor from taking a category. What they do is make Kalbe the default partner for external principals and the default supplier for a national insurer that needs volume everywhere at once [S0][S3].

The Indonesian pharmaceutical industry is growing at a rate that makes the current margin panic look temporary. The chemicals, pharmaceuticals and traditional-medicine industry grew 8.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the coordinating ministry, driven by completed chemical investments and by pharmaceutical capacity expansion aimed at the national health insurance programme [S8]. The same source frames the policy direction clearly: the government is pushing the industry to expand so that it can supply BPJS Kesehatan, which is both a demand guarantee and a price constraint [S8].

Demand is structurally supported and structurally price-capped at the same time. A national insurer covering the majority of the population guarantees volume for generic medicines, but it negotiates those volumes, and generic e-catalogue pricing is the reason the prescription division's growth trails the group even in a good year [S3]. The growth premium therefore sits in consumer health, nutrition and specialty products sold outside the reimbursement system, which is exactly where management is directing investment [S3][S6]. This is the central industry tension an investor in Kalbe has to underwrite: the state guarantees the patient base and compresses the price of the products that serve it.

Regulation is shifting in the industry's favour at the margin. The food and drug regulator obtained WHO Listed Authority status in December 2025 for vaccine regulation, a recognition that should lower friction for Indonesian-made products in export markets and improve the country's standing as a manufacturing location [S9]. The regulator is explicitly repositioning itself as an investment catalyst rather than only a gatekeeper, and is hosting an international regulatory forum in Bali in early December 2026 with regulators and companies from many countries [S9]. For Kalbe, a producer with export ambitions in vaccines and biologics, that is a slow-moving positive on the addressable market and on the credibility of its manufacturing.

The cost side is less friendly. Active pharmaceutical ingredients and packaging are substantially imported, which is why the rupiah is the single most important macro variable for the sector's margin line [S12]. Management is clear that local active-ingredient supply is limited for prescription drugs, so domestic-content strategy works in medical devices and assembly but not in the core pharmaceutical chain [S12]. The practical consequence is that the industry's gross margin moves with the exchange rate in a way that is unusual for a consumer-facing sector, and that a weak rupiah transmits into earnings within one or two quarters through inventory costs.

Competition is fragmented but stratified. Kalbe is the scale leader; the state-owned and mid-sized generic producers compete on JKN volume at lower margins, and the consumer-health categories face both local brand owners and imported brands. We do not have a single sourced market-share series in the pack, so we treat the leadership claim qualitatively: Kalbe's advantage is visible in the fact that it can carry a national distribution business as a profit centre and still grow it on third-party volume [S3]. A smaller manufacturer cannot replicate that economics.

Indonesian pharmacy retail is dominated by independent stores and chains rather than by a handful of national retailers, and reach into those outlets is built through distributor relationships and sales forces rather than through shelf-space contracts. That structure rewards the largest distributor with the widest product basket, because a pharmacy can source most of its stock from one partner. It also means that brand investment and distribution density reinforce each other: a strong brand gets shelf space, and shelf space makes the next brand launch cheaper. This is general industry background, not a sourced claim about Kalbe's current share.

The five forces are mixed. Supplier power is high and rising, because imported ingredients are concentrated and denominated in dollars, which is the heart of the current margin problem [S12]. Buyer power is high on the JKN side, where a single national payer sets generic prices, and moderate in consumer channels where brands matter. The threat of new entrants is low in manufacturing, given regulatory approval and scale, and higher in consumer health where contract manufacturing lowers the barrier. Substitutes are a real force in consumer health, where private-label and imported supplements compete on price. Rivalry is intense in generics and moderate in brands. On balance the industry structure supports a scale incumbent earning a return above its cost of capital, but not a high-margin one, which is consistent with the mid-teens return on equity Kalbe reports rather than the premium margins of a branded-consumer peer.

The external influences we monitor are the exchange rate path, JKN reimbursement policy, and the regulatory stance on drug pricing and local content. The macro deck underlying this model assumes a rupiah that stays weak through the forecast, which is why we do not model a margin recovery driven by currency; the recovery we do model comes from price and mix [S12][S0].

The historical record is one of steady top-line growth interrupted by two margin shocks. Revenue rose from IDR28,933.5bn in FY2022A to IDR35,324.5bn in FY2025A, while net profit went from IDR3,382.2bn to IDR3,665.0bn — a much flatter path, because FY2023A absorbed an input-cost squeeze and FY2024A only partly recovered [S0]. The FY2025A year was the good one: revenue growth of 8.3%, a gross margin of 39.8% and an operating margin of 12.9% produced earnings per share of Rp81 and a return on equity of 15.9% [S0].

Our forecast starts from the last actual and from the company's own operating evidence. For FY2026E we model revenue growth of 9.5%, which is below the 11.5% recorded in the first nine months because the third quarter decelerated as the comparison base normalised [S3][S0]. That produces revenue of IDR38,680.4bn and an operating profit of IDR4,680.3bn, a margin of 12.1% against 12.9% in FY2025A. The bridge is built from the reported nine months, not from a hoped-for second half: the reported nine-month gross margin was a little below thirty-eight per cent and the nine-month cost base implies an opex ratio materially below the FY2025A level [S0]. Carrying that margin flat through a Q4 at about the third quarter's run-rate gives a full-year gross margin of 37.7% against 39.8% — no Q4 uplift is assumed, because management says the pressure runs to the year end and that inventory delays any relief [S12]. The margin decline is therefore the whole story, and the opex ratio is the offset: we model 25.6%, which keeps the demonstrated nine-month efficiency rather than assuming more — the errors in the first draft offset each other, and this one does not.

The operating-expense ratio is the offset. Management reports that net margin improved even as gross margin fell, because the operating-expense ratio to sales declined [S3]. We model 25.6% easing gradually, which keeps the last actual cost base in real terms and credits only the efficiency the company has already demonstrated. The result is that earnings per share are roughly flat in FY2026E at Rp81 on revenue growth of 9.5% [S0]. The flat full year is a base effect, not deterioration: the first nine months grew sales 11.5% with the net margin rising on a lower opex ratio [S3], and the comparison is against an unusually strong fourth quarter of FY2025 — the model's Q4 carries a lower margin than that base, which is why the year looks flat while the underlying trend through September was positive. We would rather show that arithmetic than sell a trough the reported quarters do not support.

Beyond FY2026E the model assumes a partial margin recovery rather than a full one. Gross margin reaches 39.0% by FY2030E, still below the FY2025A level, driven by selective consumer price increases and the portfolio shift to specialty and biologic products that management describes [S12]. Revenue growth fades from 8.0% to 6.5% as the distribution division's external-principal boost matures, and long-run growth is 6.5%. We do not assume a rupiah reversal, because the macro deck does not forecast one [S0].

Cash flow is the part of the story the market is ignoring. Capital expenditure was IDR809.9bn in FY2025A, a low intensity for a manufacturer, and the FY2026 capex plan is under review with working capital prioritised, so we model capex of IDR967.0bn or 2.5% of sales [S10]. Working capital is the offset: net working capital is IDR10,056.9bn, about 26.0% of revenue, because management is deliberately carrying more inventory and receivables to secure imported inputs against supply disruption [S3][S10]. Even so, free cash flow to the firm is IDR1,825.8bn, and it rises as the working-capital build moderates in the forecast [S0].

The balance sheet is a genuine strength and a reason the equity is not at risk in the bear case. The pack's 30 September 2026 position is a net cash one, with debt a small fraction of cash [S0], and the model keeps it that way: FY2026E cash of IDR5,497.1bn against debt of IDR297.3bn and equity of IDR26,033.2bn, all year-end forecasts rather than the reported date, as the table labels them. The dividend, the buyback and the capex programme are therefore all funded internally; the buyback disclosure confirms internal funding and quantifies the foregone interest income as immaterial [S4]. A net-cash balance sheet does not protect the share price in a de-rating, but it does remove solvency and refinancing from the risk list, which is why our bear case is a valuation event rather than a balance-sheet event.

Capital allocation is where the base case is deliberately conservative. The FY2025 dividend resolution paid 936 IDR bn at a payout of 25.6%, well below the stated policy range that produced the FY2024 payout of 1,700 IDR bn at a payout of 52.0% [S14][S11]. The company has simultaneously been buying back stock: an earlier programme in the prior year reduced the share count, and a new programme of 500 IDR bn is running from the middle of September to the middle of December 2026 [S4][S0]. We model the last actual payout of 25.0% and a share-count reduction of -1.5% in FY2026E, so the dividend policy is upside, not embedded value.

Earnings quality is acceptable on the tests we can run, with one governance flag. The gap between net profit and operating cash flow is small relative to total assets across the last three years, which argues against accrual-driven earnings; working capital as a share of revenue has been stable to improving, and management's stated priority is to manage it down rather than let it run [S0][S10]. The flag is procedural rather than numerical: the financial regulator fined the company for not following the affiliate-transaction procedure in an asset sale and purchase between two related entities, under the applicable POJK [S5]. The amount is immaterial to value, but it is a reminder that related-party flows deserve scrutiny at this group, and we treat it as an optics-class flag rather than a manipulation-class one.

Cash conversion in pharmaceutical manufacturing is usually driven by two things: the length of the receivable cycle with hospitals and distributors, and the amount of inventory held against imported inputs. When managements say they are prioritising working capital, it normally means they are holding more inventory deliberately, which depresses near-term free cash flow but protects the production schedule. The relevant analytical question is whether the inventory build is a permanent step-up in the operating model or a temporary precaution, because only the former should be capitalised into a lower cash-flow forecast.

The FY2026E shape we are underwriting is therefore: revenue growth above the industry, a gross margin trough caused by inputs rather than demand, flat earnings per share, a working-capital build that caps free cash flow, and a net-cash balance sheet returning capital through a buyback. That is not a compounder's ideal year. It is, however, a year in which the share price already reflects something considerably worse, and the forecast is built to be beaten if the rupiah stabilises rather than to be missed if it does not [S0].

We value Kalbe primarily on discounted cash flow, because the business has a visible cash-generating operating model, a net-cash balance sheet and a forecast horizon over which margins normalise; a multiple-based target would capitalise the current trough margin at a trough multiple and double-count the pessimism. The DCF is built in nominal rupiah on free cash flow to the firm, with a cost of capital of 12.0% and terminal growth of 4.0% [S0]. That discount rate sits inside the house band for Indonesian equities; the build-up is shown below, and the beta is the industry parameter for pharmaceuticals rather than a company-specific regression we could not source.

The cost of equity is 12.0%, built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5% and a levered beta of 0.70, plus a small premium for the concentration of the shareholder register [S0]. The company's debt is trivial relative to equity — a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.01 — so the weighted cost of capital is effectively the cost of equity. We checked the result against the house band and it sits at the upper half, which is appropriate for a name with a controlling family shareholder and a thin free float rather than for a utility-like defensive.

The primary method produces Rp1,097 a share and an enterprise value of IDR45,477.8bn, with terminal value at 52.3% of the total [S0]. That terminal share is moderate for a DCF and tells us the value is not hostage to the terminal assumption; the explicit forecast carries the majority of the number. On the multiple-survival test, we state the answer rather than assert it: the implied exit EV/EBITDA is modestly above the multiple the market pays for Kalbe today, so the terminal value does contain a small re-rating, of the order of a tenth of the exit multiple. We accept it because the exit margin is assumed to recover only to the FY2025A level, not above it, and the terminal growth rate is below the industry's current nominal growth [S0][S8] — but a reader should know that roughly half the DCF is terminal value and that the terminal year is priced slightly better than the entry year, which is the one place the method is generous.

The cross-checks are shown below and they disagree with the primary, which we prefer to state plainly rather than smooth. The weights follow comparability: a capital-structure-neutral EV/EBITDA gets more than a P/E built on peer earnings we have just called distressed. The P/E method values Kalbe at Rp644 using a peer median of 7.7x, and EV/EBITDA at Rp832 using 6.7x [S0]. Both are far below the DCF — the P/E method by -41.3% and EV/EBITDA by -24.1%. The reason is the peer set: the Indonesian listed pharmaceutical universe includes state-linked and sub-scale generic producers whose earnings are depressed or whose balance sheets carry distress, so the median multiple is a distressed multiple rather than a quality multiple [S0]. Applying it to Kalbe assumes the company deserves no premium for its net cash, its distribution franchise or its consumer brands, which is precisely the assumption the market is making and the one we are challenging.

We have deliberately not anchored the cross-check on Kalbe's own five-year average, which runs from the high twenties in FY2022A to the mid-teens in FY2025A [S0]. That average is inflated by the premium-multiple period the stock has since given back, and the house method card treats the de-rating of premium IDX franchises as the base rate; using the old average would smuggle the bubble back into the target. The peer median is the conservative choice, and it is why the blended target sits below the DCF value rather than above it. The weighted target is Rp1,044 before scenario weighting and Rp1,059 after it, a total return of 43.0% including the dividend [S0].

Sensitivity is concentrated in two inputs, as it should be for this business. The gross margin path is the largest single driver, because a hundred basis points on a revenue base of this size moves operating profit by more than the buyback returns; the second is the discount rate, where a one-point change in the cost of equity moves the DCF value by a visible margin. Volume growth matters less than either, because the operating leverage in the model is modest at the margin — the company's cost base is largely fixed in the short run, so the revenue line converts to profit at a stable incremental rate. The table shows the grid; the practical reading is that the target is not sensitive enough to growth to justify a growth-led thesis, and is sensitive enough to margin to justify monitoring the gross margin line every quarter.

What does today's price imply? At Rp755 the market pays 9.3x for FY2026E earnings and 6.0x for EBITDA, with a dividend yield of 2.7% and a free-cash-flow yield of 5.6% [S0]. Those are multiples a buyer pays for a business expected to shrink. The price sits below the base-case value and below the DCF, but — the point the first draft got wrong — the forward-rolled bear value of Rp858 is above it, and the spot bear value of Rp775 is the number a bear scenario is actually worth today. The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket the price because the price is below even a zero-growth DCF, so we do not report an implied growth rate; what the price implies is a required return above the cost of capital on the nine-month run-rate, and closing that gap is the thesis.

The largest risk is the exchange rate, and it is not diversifiable within this name. Production costs are heavily import-linked, management says the margin pressure lasts through the end of FY2026, and inventory means the pass-through is delayed rather than avoided [S12]. A rupiah that stays weak for longer than the macro deck assumes would keep gross margin near the bear-case level, and because the market is already nervous about the currency, the share price would likely react before the reported margin does. We rate this high likelihood of persistence over the next two quarters and medium impact on intrinsic value, because the company can pass some of it through selective price increases [S12].

The second risk is JKN generic pricing. The state insurer guarantees volume but negotiates price, and the prescription division already grows more slowly than the group [S3][S8]. A new e-catalogue round with deeper cuts would hit the division that carries the company's identity, and it would be difficult to offset in consumer channels within a year. We rate this medium likelihood and medium impact: the policy direction is toward expanding access, which cuts both ways for a volume supplier.

The third risk is competitive. Consumer health and nutrition face imported brands and private label, and the company's own growth in those categories depends on brand rejuvenation working [S3]. A failure to rejuvenate would show up as slower consumer growth and higher marketing spend, a margin risk rather than a revenue risk. We rate it medium likelihood and low-to-medium impact.

The fourth is execution on the specialty strategy. Oncology, biosimilars and vaccines require capital, regulatory approval and time, and the payoff is beyond our explicit forecast [S6]. If those programmes slip, the mix shift that supports the margin recovery does not happen, and the base case becomes the bull case that did not arrive. We rate it medium likelihood and low near-term impact, because the spending is small relative to the group.

The fifth is governance and related-party procedure. The regulator's fine for the affiliate-transaction breach is small in money terms but relevant to the discount rate a minority holder should demand [S5]. The group's listed distribution subsidiary creates a permanent related-party flow, and any future transaction between the two would need to be judged on procedure as well as price. We rate it low likelihood of a value-destructive event and low-to-medium impact through the discount rate rather than the cash flows.

The sixth is liquidity and index positioning. The free float is 38.0% with insiders at 65.0%, and average daily traded value is IDR49.2bn [S0]. That is liquid enough for institutional positions, but a concentrated register means the shares can move on flows as much as on fundamentals, which is part of why the stock sits near its fifty-two-week low of 655.0 against a high of 1,285.0 [S0].

The scenarios are mirrored by construction. The bear case adds a negative shock to revenue growth and to gross margin; the bull case adds the same magnitude in the opposite direction, with a narrative built on the same drivers [S0]. The bear case is not a catastrophe but it is no longer decorative: it adds a JKN e-catalogue price cut and a rupiah that stays weak, taking gross margin below the nine-month level as the table's shocks show, halves growth and raises the required return as the market de-rates a policy-exposed family franchise. It produces a value of Rp858 today, above the price — we say so plainly rather than engineering a lower number. The value at the peer median of 7.7x, Rp644, is the only cross-check below the price, and we reject it as a distressed-earnings multiple. The bull case mirrors the bear and produces Rp1,291. We re-ran the weighting with the bear at double its base probability: the target falls but remains above the price, so the BUY is a statement about the DCF's long-run margin path, not about the probabilities. A reader who believes the JKN cut and the de-rating together are the most likely path should own the peer-median value, not our target, and that is the disagreement worth having.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A quarterly gross margin that stabilises while revenue keeps growing would confirm the trough and pull the DCF toward the upper end of the sensitivity grid. A dividend decision at the FY2026 annual meeting that returns to the stated policy range would lift the payout line and signal management's confidence in cash generation [S11]. Conversely, a JKN price round that cuts generic reimbursement, or a rupiah that breaks well beyond the macro deck's path, would move us toward the bear case and force a re-underwrite of the margin recovery rather than a simple markdown.

Ownership and control are concentrated in the founding family, with the pack's insider series at 65.0% against a registry free float of 38.0% — overlapping definitions, not additive [S0]. The board is professionalised, with a president director and directors who run the operating divisions, and the company has a corporate secretary and investor-relations function that discloses promptly [S4][S11]. There is no evidence in the sources we reviewed of pledged controlling shares, a serial rights issue or a beneficial-ownership structure that obscures control; the register is simple and the controlling shareholder is known.

The governance flag we do carry is the financial regulator's administrative sanction for an affiliate-transaction procedure breach. The company and its listed distribution subsidiary were fined in connection with an asset sale and purchase between two related entities, with the regulator finding that the affiliate-transaction procedure under the applicable POJK was not followed [S5]. The fine itself is immaterial — we record it as a fact of 0.2 IDR bn — but the finding is a procedure finding, and procedure findings at family-controlled groups are worth tracking because they are the leading indicator of value leakage. We classify it as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed, it is quantified, and there is no allegation of fictitious revenue or fabricated cash.

Related-party gravity is structural at this group. The distribution subsidiary is listed and minority-held, so a meaningful share of group profit is earned in an entity that also transacts with the parent [S0]. The company has said it may delist that subsidiary if it cannot meet the free-float requirement [S12], which would be a related-party transaction of a different order of magnitude if it happens. We assign it no value: an EPMT buy-in would be a cash outflow negotiated with the controlling shareholder, no terms are announced, and any number we put on it would be a guess about the price paid to minorities rather than a valuation. The minority leakage is already deducted at book in the DCF bridge, so a buy-in at book would be value-neutral before the cash cost; it belongs on the monitoring list, judged on the price paid rather than the strategic rationale.

The dividend record is good but has one anomaly. The FY2024 distribution was 1,700 IDR bn, a payout of 52.0% that sat inside the company's stated policy range, and the shares have paid a cash dividend every year in the data pack [S11][S0]. The FY2025 resolution paid 936 IDR bn at a payout of 25.6%, below the stated policy, at the same time as the company was buying back stock and prioritising working capital [S14][S4]. A lower dividend alongside a buyback can be rational capital allocation, but it is a departure from a stated policy, and we treat a return to the policy as an upside catalyst rather than as the base case.

On ESG, the material exposures are product quality and pharmacovigilance, which the regulator supervises and which the WHO Listed Authority status bears on [S9]; access to medicines, where the JKN generic supply is a positive social contribution but a margin constraint [S8]; and packaging and input sourcing, where imported active ingredients and local-content rules are the live policy issues [S12]. The company's environmental footprint is a manufacturing footprint, and we have no sourced emissions or waste data in the pack, so we do not make claims about it. We would rather say the data is thin than invent a score.

The dated catalysts are the buyback window closing in the middle of December 2026, which removes a persistent bid and tests the price on fundamentals [S4]; the international regulatory forum in Bali in early December, which is a platform for the regulator's investment narrative rather than a direct earnings event [S9]; the FY2026 audited results and FY2027 guidance at the end of the first quarter of 2027, where the gross margin line is the number that matters [S3]; and the annual general meeting in the second quarter of 2027, where the dividend decision against the stated policy is the cleanest signal of management's confidence [S11].

Between those dates the KPIs we watch are the quarterly gross margin, the operating-expense ratio, the growth of the distribution division's external-principal business, the working-capital ratio, and the share count under the buyback. The gross margin is first among equals: it is the line where the rupiah, the input costs and the mix shift all meet, and it is the line that decides whether the base case or the bear case is right. We will update the model on each quarterly report, and we will re-underwrite the margin path if two consecutive quarters show no stabilisation [S0].

The monitoring list also includes the regulator's follow-through on the affiliate-transaction finding and any proposal regarding the listed distribution subsidiary [S5][S12]. Neither is likely to change the target on its own, but both change the discount rate we apply to a family-controlled register, and the discount rate is the second-largest input in the valuation after the margin path.

We are initiating with a BUY, a target of Rp1,059 and a total return of 43.0%, on a base case that assumes the margin trough is FY2026E, growth continues across all four divisions, and capital is returned through a buyback while the dividend policy stays conservative. The bear case is a valuation event, not a solvency event, and the price sits below it. That is the asymmetry we are underwriting [S0].

bear.narrative: The JKN e-catalogue round cuts generic reimbursement while the rupiah stays near Rp18,500/USD, so gross margin falls about 2.5pp below the 9M 2026 level to 35.2% and growth halves as volume chases price; the required return rises 75bp as the market de-rates a policy-exposed family franchise, and the multiple stays at the peer trough rather than recovering.

bull.narrative: The rupiah stabilises and raw-material costs ease, the specialty/biologic and oncology portfolio plus selective price increases restore gross margin 2.5pp above the 9M 2026 level, growth adds 2.5pp as the distribution arm keeps winning external principals, and the required return falls 75bp as the policy-exposure discount unwinds.

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 9.5%: 9M 2026 net sales were +11.5% YoY with every segment positive [S3], H1 2026 was +14.04% to Rp19.47tn [S12], and Q3 2026 revenue of Rp9,495bn implies about +6.5% YoY as the comparison base normalises, so the year lands near 9.5%. FY2027E 8.0%: management entered 2026 targeting above its 6-8% range and the industry (chemicals, pharma, traditional medicine) grew 8.1% in Q3 2026 [S6][S8]. FY2028E 7.5%, FY2029E 7.0%, FY2030E 6.5%: fade toward the industry's nominal rate as the distribution third-party-principal boost (+21.6% in 9M 2026 [S3]) matures. Long-run 5.0%: real pharma volume plus a 3% inflation path, below the 8.1% current industry rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 37.7%: the reported nine months were 37.63% (gross profit Rp10,903.7bn on revenue Rp28,974.0bn, S0 quarterlies), so the full year needs only a flat Q4 at about 37.8% — no margin recovery is assumed, consistent with management saying the pressure lasts to end-2026 and that inventory delays any relief [S3][S12]. FY2027E 38.4% and then +20bp a year to 39.0% by FY2030E: only a partial recovery toward the 39.8% actually earned in FY2025, driven by selective consumer price increases and the portfolio shift to higher-margin specialty/biologic products that management is executing [S12]; it does not assume a rupiah reversal, which the macro deck does not forecast.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 25.6% in FY2026E, easing 10bp a year to 25.2%: the reported nine months imply an opex ratio of about 25.6% (gross profit Rp10,903.7bn less interest income and a PBT of Rp3,661bn on revenue of Rp28,974.0bn, S0 quarterlies), and the company states the net margin improved because the operating-expense ratio to sales fell [S3], which management attributes to digitalisation and marketing effectiveness [S3]. The FY2025 actual was 26.9%, so this keeps the last actual's cost base in real terms with only the demonstrated efficiency.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2022-FY2025 data-pack average of about 1.04% of sales [S0]. The annual-report notes that would let us restate depreciation from the fixed-asset schedule could not be retrieved (the Kalbe investor site renders client-side), so this line is not restated; it is flagged as a residual data risk rather than modelled around.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 2.5%: the 2026 plan was about Rp1trn, roughly 2.6% of forecast sales, but management is reviewing it and prioritising working capital, with spend redirected to pharma and nutrition capacity [S10]. FY2027E-FY2030E 2.6%: the planned capacity additions in pharma and nutrition [S10] at a lower intensity than the 3.3% three-year average, consistent with the 2.3% actually spent in FY2025 [S0].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 26.0% of sales, against 25.8% at 30 September 2026 (nwc Rp9,891bn on LTM sales Rp38,310bn) [S0]. Management is deliberately holding more inventory and receivables to secure imported raw materials and packaging against supply disruption, and names working capital as the 2026 priority [S10][S3], so the ratio is held flat rather than released.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22.5%, the Indonesian statutory corporate rate and the three-year average the data pack implies [S0]; no tax holiday or loss carry-forward is disclosed in the sources reviewed.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Kept at the data-pack three-year average of 7.5%; gross debt is only Rp294bn at 30 September 2026 [S0], so the line is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Kept at the data-pack three-year average of 3.7% on an average cash balance of about Rp5trn [S0]; the buyback disclosure quantifies only Rp8.4bn of foregone interest income [S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company is in a net cash position (debt Rp294bn against cash Rp5,579bn at 30 September 2026) [S0] and funds capex, dividends and the Rp500bn buyback from internal cash [S4].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the sources reviewed disclose no recurring non-operating income line; interest income is modelled through the cash-yield input [S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: LTM net profit of Rp3,887bn against Rp3,770bn attributable to parent holders implies about 3.0% to minorities [S0], mainly the listed distribution subsidiary EPMT. Held flat; no minority buy-out is announced, only an option to delist EPMT if it cannot meet the free-float rule [S12].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 25%: the FY2025 dividend resolution paid Rp936.26bn, 25.6% of the Rp3.66tn FY2025 net profit, DPS Rp20, cum date 3 June 2026 [S14], below the company's stated 45-55% policy that produced the 52% FY2024 payout of Rp1.7trn [S11]. The base case keeps the resolved FY2025 payout rather than the policy, because the company is retaining cash for working capital and the buyback [S10][S4]; a return to policy is upside in the bull case, not the base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: -1.5% in FY2026E only: the company is buying back up to Rp500bn between 17 September and 17 December 2026 [S4], about 1.5% of the Rp34.1trn market value; the FY2025 buyback reduced shares from 45,951m to 45,287m over the year [S0]. Zero thereafter: the mandate expires on 17 December 2026 and no new programme is disclosed, so the share count is held flat from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: real volume of about 1% plus the 3.3% CPI path in the house macro deck [S0], not a haircut to the operating forecast. It sits below Indonesian nominal GDP and below the 8.1% current industry rate [S8] because roughly half the book — JKN generics sold through the prescription division — is price-administered by the national insurer and cannot grow at the nominal GDP rate; the un-capped consumer and distribution halves grow faster and carry the forecast's explicit growth. Mature-market pharma terminal growth is the right anchor for the capped half.
